title: How South Korea keeps most of its food waste out of landfills
description:
Globally more than a billion tonnes of food is wasted each year and much of it ends up in landfills. As the food breaks down it releases huge amounts of methane, making up 10% of the world’s climate-warming emissions. Now many cities and governments are looking to South Korea as a model of how to reduce food waste and boost food recycling.

BBC reporter Soo Min Kim explains how South Korea cut household food waste going to landfill from 97% to almost nothing. Among other things, they’ve nudged the public to think about their food waste by making it mandatory to separate food waste and to pay for throwing it away. The country also has special RFID bins to handle disposal and payments, and there are financial penalties for people who don’t comply.

We also hear from content creators around the world about how they reduce their food waste. They are: Senjuti Chakraborty in India, Debbi Love in the UK, and Chatty Miss Maddie and Lani Marschall in Australia. Plus BBC reporter William Lee Adams shares some of the surprising food saving hacks he came across on social media.

summaryEn: This episode of What in the World explores how South Korea transformed its food waste management system, reducing household food waste sent to landfills from 97% to nearly zero. BBC reporter Soo-Min Kim details the country's strict policies, including mandatory waste separation, pay-as-you-throw RFID smart bins, designated disposal bags, penalties, and municipal incentive schemes. She explains how collected food waste is repurposed into animal feed, fertilizer, and bioenergy—such as at the Daejeon Bio Energy Center—preventing harmful methane emissions. Additionally, content creators from around the world and BBC reporter William Lee Adams share practical food-saving hacks, including preserving lettuce, making kiwi skin kimchi, and freezing portioned garlic and tomato paste in ice cube trays.
